title: Data
text:
Dataset configs
Each config/<dataset>_config.yml describes one matrix: where its data is, how to build it, and each method’s parameter grid. Subsets analysed separately (e.g. one timepoint) are separate configs, each with its own dataset.id; there’s no “several matrices in one config”. config/dataset_metadata.example.yml is a fully commented template. Configs are read and validated by read_dataset_metadata() / validate_dataset_metadata() (R/lib/metadata.R).
To add a dataset:

Write config/<dataset>_config.yml (copy the example).
Add its dataset.id to datasets: in config/pipeline.yml.
Run the pipeline. Only the new dataset’s targets are built.

File names needn’t match ids (ANEMONES_day1_config.yml declares ANEMONES_DAY1); the pipeline finds a config by its declared dataset.id.
The dataset: block:







Key
Meaning




id
unique dataset id, used in target and DB names


description
free text


expression_path
long-format expression parquet (feature id, sample id, value)


sample_metadata_path, feature_metadata_path
sample and feature metadata parquets


sample_id_col, feature_id_col, value_col
column names in those files


ensembl_col
feature-metadata column holding Ensembl gene ids – the cross-dataset identifier (below)


symbol_col
optional; feature-metadata column of gene symbols, for display only


subject_id_col
optional; sample-metadata column naming each sample’s subject (person). Links a person’s samples across a family’s datasets and keeps them together when fits resample (fit_subjects(), R/targets/run_method_fit.R); a design: block’s subject takes precedence


matrix_path / preprocessing_script
how the matrix is built (below)



feature_id_col must match the column of feature_metadata_path whose values equal the matrix’s row names.
The methods: block holds each method’s parameter grid; see Methods. A method runs for a dataset only if it appears there.

The design: block
Optional. A dataset with one gets the repeated-measures analysis (variance partition, dream, composition and sex checks; see Methods). Read by validate_design() and prepare_design() (R/lib/design.R). Column names refer to the sample metadata and must be syntactic R names.







Field
Meaning




platform
array (log-scale values, one probe per symbol, no variance filter) or rnaseq (counts → filterByExpr() → TMM → voom weights)


subject
person id; omit for a cross-sectional dataset


time, time_order
timepoint column and its levels in chronological order (required with time)


group
arm or subphenotype; cells are group × time


group_at_first_time
true: every sample takes its subject’s first-timepoint group (a status that changes over time, e.g. GSE13904’s “SIRS resolved”)


covariates
further variables in the variance model; categorical ones are random effects


vp_covariates
numeric covariates for the variance model only (e.g. ROSE’s sequencing QC)


numeric
which covariates are numeric (fixed effects, standardized)


de_covariates
fixed-effect covariates added to the dream model


drop, keep
{column: [values]} sample filters


set_na, recode
{column: [values]} recoded to missing; {column: {from: to}}


contrasts
cross-sectional only: {name: "levelA - levelB"}; default every group pair


control_probes
the array’s control probes for the composition check: {id_pattern: "<regex>"} or {column: <feature-metadata column>, values: [...]}; with covariate: true their first principal component enters the variance and dream models (compute_control_factor(), R/lib/expression.R)



"NA", "" and NA are missing; samples missing any model variable are dropped and counted. Per-timepoint subsets have no design: block: their factors are described with their parent’s design (variance_parent(), R/targets/variance.R).
Composition markers. config/composition_markers.yml lists the neutrophil and lymphocyte marker genes behind the per-sample composition scores (analyze_composition(), R/targets/composition.R). Editing it reruns only the composition targets and what reads them.


YAML keys that are booleans
R’s yaml package reads an unquoted key that is a YAML 1.1 boolean token – y, n, yes, no, on, off, true, false, in any capitalization – as TRUE/FALSE, not the string you wrote. A method argument literally named n silently becomes the key FALSE. read_dataset_metadata() errors on a TRUE/FALSE key under methods:; quote such keys ("n": [...]).

title: Data
text:
Building a matrix
The pipeline never assumes a normalization or metadata values. load_input_matrix() (R/lib/matrices.R) builds the matrix one of three ways, first match wins:








#
Config
Behavior




1
dataset.matrix_path
reads that RDS matrix as-is


2
dataset.preprocessing_script
runs your script against the raw parquet trio


3
neither
pivots expression_path wide – no normalization, no filtering



Every current dataset uses a preprocessing script (R/preprocessing/<dataset>_preprocessing.R), run by run_preprocessing_script() (R/lib/matrices.R). The result must be a plain matrix with row names = feature ids and column names = sample ids. Any sample or gene filtering belongs in the script (or the prebuilt matrix).

Preprocessing-script contract
The script is source()d with these variables already defined:







Variable
From




expression_path, sample_metadata_path, feature_metadata_path
dataset.*_path


sample_id_col, feature_id_col, value_col, ensembl_col
dataset.*_col


tmp_dir
a directory created for this run



It must write its feature × sample matrix to file.path(tmp_dir, "matrix.rds"). To also run it by hand, guard on tmp_dir, which only exists when the pipeline sources the script:
framework_run <- exists("tmp_dir", inherits = FALSE)
if (!framework_run) {
  expression_path <- "~/local/path/to/expression.parquet"   # ... etc.
}
# ... your logic ...
if (framework_run) saveRDS(final_mat, file.path(tmp_dir, "matrix.rds"))
The one transform the pipeline applies itself is the non-negativity shift NMF and CoGAPS need (shift_nonneg(), the mat_nn_<dataset> target): an algorithm requirement, not a normalization choice.

title: Data
text:
Dataset families
config/dataset_families.yml lists which datasets are timepoints or subsets of the same cohort (e.g. ANEMONES and ANEMONES_DAY1…ANEMONES_DISCHARGE). It decides two things:

projectR intercept: projections within a family leave out the intercept; projections across families include it.
Gene-space agreement is computed between datasets in the same family only.

Families are listed explicitly, not inferred from dataset-id naming.

title: Data
text:
Gene identifiers across datasets
Each dataset’s matrix keeps its platform’s own feature ids (Illumina/Affymetrix probes, Entrez ids, versioned Ensembl ids). Anything that compares datasets or gene sets – enrichment and projectR – first remaps row names to version-stripped Ensembl gene ids (ENSG00000001234.2 → ENSG00000001234) with build_ensembl_map()/remap_to_ensembl() (R/lib/ingest/symbol_mapping.R), using dataset.ensembl_col. Several probes mapping to one gene are collapsed; a ;-separated multi-gene entry takes its first gene.
Gene symbols (build_symbol_map(), dataset.symbol_col) are for display only, never for matching: symbols are ambiguous and renamed across annotation releases.
A dataset with a missing or wrong ensembl_col keeps its native ids, so it matches almost nothing in other datasets. That shows up not as an error but as near-zero n_genes_matched in projections (projectR logs “0 row names matched”).

Which datasets are built
config/pipeline.yml lists the 35 datasets the pipeline builds: 12 full datasets (11 with a design: block; SHIP-TREND has no sample metadata) and 23 per-timepoint subsets. One config is left out:







Dataset
Why




gains
R/preprocessing/gains_preprocessing.R is an unfinished stub: it reads the four sub-cohort expression files (E-MTAB-4421/4451/5273/5274) but never builds a matrix. Whether to pool the four accessions is still undecided.



SHIP-TREND (991 healthy samples) has no sample metadata (its phenotype data is access-restricted): it gets factor fits but no design, variance or composition analysis.

title: Database
text:
The pipeline writes a SQLite database at db_path in config/pipeline.yml (default results/stability.sqlite). Bulky results – loadings, scores, diagnostics, raw model objects, projections – are files under stability_artifacts/<dataset_id>/ next to it, referenced by paths relative to the DB’s directory, so the two move together.
It is a derived output. Every row is rebuilt from the targets store; nothing is edited by hand and there are no migrations.

db_<dataset> (write_dataset_db(), R/targets/db_write.R) writes everything about one dataset in one transaction.
db_cross_dataset (write_cross_dataset_db()) then writes the tables linking two datasets (projections, gene-space agreement) and deletes artifact files no row references.
Other targets produce rows keyed by fit_key (dataset + method + parameters); the writers resolve keys to integer ids. Fits are upserted on fit_key, so a fit keeps its fit_id across rewrites.

Schema versioning. The schema is R/db/schema.sql and R/db/views.sql; open_stability_db() (R/db/connect.R) creates them on a new file and stamps PRAGMA user_version with SCHEMA_VERSION. It refuses a DB with a different version. After any schema change, bump SCHEMA_VERSION, delete the DB and its stability_artifacts/, and run tar_make(); only the ingestion and DB targets rerun.
What it holds. The schema-1 build of 30 datasets (2026-10-05) had 7,990 fits in 3.6 GB; the largest tables were match_scores (8.9 M rows), gene_modules (3.3 M), factor_matches (3.0 M) and enrichment_results (2.1 M). Schema 2 moved the two bulkiest contents out of the tables: the enrichment gene lists (about 1.1 GB) and the pattern markers (4.6 M rows) are now per-dataset artifacts (enrichment_genes, pattern_markers).
Reading it. Open read-only from R with DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), path, flags = RSQLite::SQLITE_RO), or sqlite3 -readonly. Whole-table scans of the 3.6 GB file over the cluster’s network filesystem are slow from a login node; copy it to a compute node’s local disk for heavy queries.



Stability without every cell. For each pair of fits of a method, factors are matched 1-to-1 (Hungarian algorithm on loadings cosine; on |cosine| for methods whose factors can flip sign). Rather than store every factor × factor similarity (85% of which were never read), the DB keeps the matches plus context to judge them: each match’s runner-up and margin, statistics of the unmatched similarities per fit pair, and pooled histograms.
WGCNA kME in context. For each gene, its correlation with its own module’s eigengene (kME), its best competing module, an analytic p-value, and an empirical p-value against a permutation null (each eigengene’s samples shuffled 100 times), with member / non-member / permutation summaries and histograms per module. The full genes × modules kME matrix is an artifact.
Everything computed is kept, including tables the app doesn’t read yet (pattern drivers, markers, redundancy, ICASSO membership, the diagnostics).
Method-specific values in long tables (fit_params, fit_metrics, fit_artifacts) rather than per-method columns.
Enrichment is stored separately from its jobs. Each enrichment branch keeps its result trimmed to the significant terms; rows are built afterwards, so changing these tables never reruns fgsea.

title: Database
text:
Conventions

Engine: SQLite. Column types are SQLite storage classes: INTEGER, REAL, TEXT.
Booleans are INTEGER with CHECK (x IN (0,1)).
Timestamps are TEXT in ISO-8601 UTC (utc_now(), e.g. 2026-10-05T16:13:15Z).
Creation: the schema is defined in R/db/schema.sql (tables) and R/db/views.sql (views). open_stability_db() in R/db/connect.R creates them on a new DB and stamps PRAGMA user_version. An existing DB with a different version is refused; delete it and rebuild. There are no migrations.
Connection pragmas: foreign_keys = ON, journal_mode = WAL, synchronous = NORMAL, busy_timeout = 30000.
Who writes: the DB is written by two deployment = "main" targets only.

db_<dataset>, via write_dataset_db() in R/targets/db_write.R, writes every table scoped to one dataset in a single transaction.
db_cross_dataset, via write_cross_dataset_db() in R/targets/db_write.R, writes the tables that link two datasets (projections, gene_space_agreement).
Every other target computes in-memory rows keyed by fit_key (and factor_index). The writer resolves those keys to integer ids.

Update semantics:

datasets and fits are upserted. fits is matched on fit_key, so a fit keeps its fit_id across rewrites.
All child rows of a dataset are deleted and re-inserted on each write.
Fits whose fit_key disappeared are deleted, and ON DELETE CASCADE removes their dependents.

Abbreviations below: PK primary key, FK → t.c foreign key, CASCADE = ON DELETE CASCADE, UQ part of a UNIQUE constraint, NN NOT NULL, IDX indexed.

title: Database
text:
Pair-stability tables
Stability compares every pair of fits of one method within a dataset (all seeds, all ranks).

Factor methods use Hungarian matching on loadings cosine (on |cosine| for sign-ambiguous methods). WGCNA matches modules by gene Jaccard.

The methods and their parameters
A method runs for a dataset when it appears under the config’s methods: block (WGCNA nests under methods.network). Each key is the underlying tool’s own argument name. Stability designs. For NMF, CoGAPS and ICA the question is whether factors recur across random seeds (and, for ICA, bootstrap resamples of subjects). PCA, sPCA and WGCNA are deterministic given their parameters, so for them the question is how structure changes as the swept parameter grows. Every method is also compared across ranks.
CoGAPS’s three sub-blocks mirror its three call sites: params goes to CogapsParams(), distributed_params to setDistributedParams(), run to CoGAPS() itself. Some argument names exist on more than one of them, so put each under the function it belongs to. nSets and nThreads default to the cogaps controller’s cpus_per_task.
Threads and identity. Parameters that only set parallelism (NMF n.threads, CoGAPS nSets/nThreads, WGCNA nThreads) are listed in the method’s resource_params and left out of a fit’s identity (fit_key).

PCA: one fit per dataset
PCA components are nested – the first k components of a rank-20 fit are the rank-k solution – so PCA is fit once per dataset, at the largest configured rank. The fit also records mse_by_rank, every truncation’s reconstruction error. Choosing the first n components is left to ingestion and the app.


sPCA: choosing the sparsity
sPCA runs with sparse = "varnum", under which para is the fraction of genes allowed a non-zero loading in each component, converted to a count from the dataset’s gene number. Fit time grows steeply with para and K: for EARLI (7465 genes × 189 samples) the median fit took 1.1 min at para 0.1 and K 2–5, but 158 min at para 0.5 and K 16–20.
How the sparsity is chosen. We follow Guerra-Urzola, Van Deun, Vera & Sijtsma (2021), “A Guide for Sparse PCA: Model Comparison and Applications”, Psychometrika 86(4):893–919 (PMC8636462): fix K, then choose the sparsity that maximizes the Index of Sparseness
IS = PEV_sparse × PEV_pca × PS

PEV_sparse: variance explained by the sparse components.
PEV_pca: variance explained by the first K ordinary principal components (from the dataset’s PCA fit).
PS: the proportion of zero loadings; under varnum, PS = 1 − para.

The authors report that IS beat cross-validation and BIC at recovering the true sparsity, with a single interior peak in their applications (97% sparsity for gene expression).
The search runs in two stages per dataset (spca_build_grid(), spca_refine_grid() in R/methods/spca.R):

Scan: one K (K_scan, default 5) at para_scan = 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5.
Refine: the scan’s IS winner p*, then every K (2–12) at p* − para_step, p* and p* + para_step (default 0.05), skipping pairs the scan already fit.

That’s about 36 fits per dataset. selection_spca_<dataset> (spca_select_fits()) tabulates IS for every fit and marks the best para per K; those fits are sPCA’s representative fits. If the scan’s winner sits at the edge of para_scan, the refinement still runs, the selection table records at_scan_edge and a warning suggests widening para_scan for that dataset. K_scan, para_scan and para_step can be set per dataset in methods: spca:.

Why one sparsity per dataset. On the earlier full grid (30 datasets, K 2–12, para 0.02–0.5; 2,968 fits, 1,451 CPU-hours) every IS winner was at para 0.25–0.50, and para ≤ 0.2 never won. The winner moved by at most 0.10 across K within a dataset but differed between datasets (GSE54514 0.25, GSE95233 0.35, ANEMONES 0.45). Replaying those fits with a scan at K = 5 and the winner ± 0.05 for every other K landed within 0.05 of each K’s winner at ≥ 80% of the Ks in all 30 datasets, losing a mean 0.004% of IS (worst 0.63%), for about half the compute. A lower scan K was noisier and a higher one costlier without agreeing better.
lambda is not swept. We tested λ ∈ {1e-6, 0.1, 1} under varnum on EARLI: across 113 (K, para) pairs fit at both 1e-6 and 1, total PEV differed by a median of 1.5e-4 and at most 5.7e-4. Under varnum, para fixes the number of non-zero loadings, leaving λ almost nothing to change (the paper makes the same point about LARS-EN). lambda is one value, default 1e-6, and spca_build_grid() rejects a list.
Convergence. spca() runs with trace = TRUE, which prints its iteration count every 10 iterations; run_spca_job() captures it and records iterations (a lower bound, to within 10) and whether max.iter was reached without converging (converged in fit_metrics; hit_max_iter in the selection table, where such fits stay, flagged).
The 8-hour stop. A fit still running after max_hours (default 8) stops itself and is recorded as failed (killed_not_converged), with the iterations it reached. On the earlier grid only two fits ended this way (ANEMONES para 0.05, K 10 and 11), in the low-para range the scan no longer covers.
Scores are computed on the centered matrix, matching how spca() fits the model.



ICA, ICASSO and kurtosis
ICA (fastICA, after a PCA prewhitening step; run_ica_seed_sweep_job() in R/methods/ica.R) is fit across seeds and, with bootstrap = TRUE, on bootstrap resamples. A resample draws subjects with replacement and takes all of each drawn subject’s samples, so a person’s repeated samples stay together; drawing single samples would leave most people in every replicate through their other samples and overstate stability. Subjects come from fit_subjects() (R/targets/run_method_fit.R, the subjects_<dataset> target); in a cross-sectional dataset every sample is its own subject, which is the ordinary bootstrap. A bootstrap fit keeps its sources under the resampled sample ids (boot_idx, boot_subjects) but has no per-sample scores.
ICASSO (Himberg, Hyvärinen & Esposito 2004, NeuroImage 22(3):1214–1222) pools every component of every fit at one rank – seeds and bootstrap resamples together – clusters them by |cosine| (average linkage, cut to the rank), and scores each cluster with Iq = mean within-cluster similarity − mean similarity to everything outside it. Iq ≥ 0.7 is the usual “trustworthy” threshold.
Per-component kurtosis (Lee & Batzoglou 2003) is the non-Gaussianity fastICA maximizes; a clearly positive excess kurtosis is the expected signature of a real biological source.


WGCNA: one network over all genes
For each soft-thresholding power, WGCNA correlates every pair of genes across samples and raises the correlations to that power, suppressing weak ones. It then computes the topological overlap (TOM) – how many strong partners two genes share – builds a gene tree from 1 − TOM, and cuts it into modules of at least minModuleSize genes. Modules whose eigengenes (first principal components) correlate above 1 − mergeCutHeight are merged.
These genes × genes matrices grow with the square of the gene count, so blockwiseModules() by default caps a network at 5,000 genes and splits larger data into blocks, building separate networks within each. Genes in different blocks are then never compared, and the block count depends on the gene count. We set maxBlockSize = 50000, so each fit is one network over all genes (about 7,500), as the WGCNA authors recommend whenever memory allows. Its gene tree is then the one the modules were cut from, and ingestion stores it directly. Workers request 6 GB for this.
Each fit (run_wgcna_param_job(), R/methods/wgcna.R) also stores every gene’s connectivity (total, within its module, outside it, and the difference; intramodularConnectivity.fromExpr()), the scale-free fit of that connectivity at the fit’s power (scaleFreeFitIndex()), and the goodSamplesGenes() result. The TOM itself (genes × genes per fit) is not saved; it can be rebuilt from the dataset’s matrix and the fit’s parameters.


Error handling and timings
Every fit function runs inside capture_fit() (R/lib/method_registry.R): a failing fit returns its error message instead of stopping its batch, and every result records its wall time. sPCA additionally stops itself at max_hours.

Adding a method
Write one R/methods/<name>.R and add a controller named <name> to config/pipeline.yml. The file defines three things.
1. A fit function that reads its matrix from the free variable mat (or mat_nn, the non-negative shift) and, if it resamples, each column’s subject from subjects; run_method_fits() (R/targets/run_method_fit.R) binds both for each call. Its arguments are the columns your build_grid() produces. Wrap the body in capture_fit() so a failure is recorded rather than stopping the batch, and return as much of the model as is cheap to store: ingestion can then change without refitting.
2. <name>_registry, the fitting contract (the variable name must match the file name):







Field
Meaning

"mat" or "mat_nn"

the fit function


build_grid
function(params) returning one row per fit, usually expand.grid() over the fit function’s arguments; params is defaults merged with the dataset config (merge_named_list())

optional default parameters

optional packages to load on the worker


resource_defaults
optional function(params, resources) for defaults from the worker’s resources (cpus_per_task)

TRUE to fit on the non-negative shift

3. <name>_ingest, the ingestion contract (validate_method_ingest()):







Field
Meaning

"seed_sweep" or "param_grid"

TRUE if factors are unique only up to sign (matching uses |similarity|; enrichment tests both ends)

Methods considered and dropped

CP and Tucker tensor decompositions (genes × subjects × timepoints) were implemented and removed on 2026-09-29. The planned data has only 2 timepoints per subject, too few to fit a time mode or choose its rank; tensor rank selection is NP-hard and CP/Tucker results are very sensitive to hyperparameters (summary).
ICAclust (Nascimento et al., PLoS One 2017) clusters genes by temporal shape with ICA over timepoints; with 2 timepoints its rotation has a single free angle, so the method is degenerate. Never adopted.
Masking cross-validation and subsample projection stability designs were explored and removed; see git history to revive them.

section: Repeated measures: variance partition, differential expression and sample checks
text:
Repeated measures: variance partition, differential expression and sample checks
Most datasets sample each patient more than once. Before deciding how the factor analysis should treat that, the pipeline measures, per gene, how expression variance splits into between-person, time and the rest (variancePartition), tests change over time (dream), and checks each dataset’s samples (leukocyte composition, technical scale, recorded vs inferred sex). It runs for every dataset with a design: block (see Data, “The design: block”) and never touches a factor fit, so it can be rebuilt on its own.

How it runs









Step
Target
Function (file)
What it does

applies the design: block: filters, recodes, standardizes numeric covariates, builds the cell factor, formulas, contrasts (build_contrasts(), makeContrastsDream()) and the canonical correlations between design variables

write_variance_artifacts(), variance_db_rows() (R/targets/variance_db.R)

To rebuild only this module, run the selection in Running the workflow (“Running the pipeline”); R/explore/variance_by_time.R plots the stored summaries interactively. Model tasks run on the vp controller (BiocParallel MulticoreParam, forked workers over its CPUs) and record their own peak memory and CPU time from the job’s cgroup.


Models
The models use each platform’s own processing, not the factor-analysis matrix (which is filtered to the top-variance genes), as the variancePartition vignettes recommend.

Variance partition (ML, as the vignette recommends for fractions): ~ (1|subject) + (1|time) + (1|group) + (1|group:time) + (1|categorical covariates) + numeric covariates. Categorical variables are random effects; numeric covariates are standardized (a fraction, var(Xβ), doesn’t depend on scale; centring keeps a coefficient off the intercept, scaling keeps lme4 from refusing predictors on very different scales). The terms fall into categories: subject, subject-level (variables fixed within a person: sex, age, arm), time, group × time, technical (vp_covariates), covariate, residual. The between-subject total is subject + subject-level, as the vignette’s nesting note says; the residual fraction is reported but not used as a metric (the vignette’s FAQ).
dream (REML; Kenward-Roger for ≤ 20 samples, else Satterthwaite): ~ 0 + cell + (1|subject) plus any de_covariates, cell = group × time. Time courses test each timepoint against the first within each group with at least 3 repeatedly sampled subjects, plus a joint F-test per group; cross-sectional datasets test group pairs. z.std and F.std make statistics comparable across genes with different degrees of freedom.
Checks: dream against duplicateCorrelation() (dupcor_<dataset>; the genome-wide consensus matches the median subject fraction), canCorPairs() between design variables, per-gene collinearity scores and singular-fit flags, and the vignettes’ plots (violin and per-gene bars, expression of each term’s top gene, correlation structure, contrast matrix, dream vs duplicateCorrelation p-values, voom trend).



Sample checks
analyze_composition() (composition_<dataset>) records, per sample:

Leukocyte composition: neutrophil and lymphocyte marker scores (config/composition_markers.yml) and their difference, against each sample’s expression spread, location and leading principal components.
A technical reference: the array’s own control probes where the platform has them (ANEMONES’ Agilent spike-ins, the Affymetrix hybridization controls), a background stand-in for Illumina series matrices (probes matching no transcript), and library size and TMM factor for RNA-seq. The same sample-level traits also go through the dataset’s variance formula.
Sex: inferred from chrY genes against XIST and compared with the recorded sex; subjects whose samples disagree are counted. This catches sample annotations that don’t belong to their arrays.

Findings (2026-10-13): in the RNA-seq time courses PC1 is the neutrophil-lymphocyte axis (|rho| 0.83–0.90), not library size. ANEMONES’ sample-mean shift follows its spike-in controls (rho 0.92), not composition, so its control probes’ first principal component enters its models as a covariate (control_probes: {covariate: true}): shifting each sample by a control offset over-corrected, because the controls move about twice as much as genes. GSE54514’s sample annotations don’t match its arrays (sex agreement 0.50; samples of one group_id disagree on sex in 35 of 54 subjects), so its subject and time results aren’t interpretable. Smaller sex discordances: ANEMONES (4 subjects), GSE95233 (Patient 198), GSE13904 and GSE273700 (1 subject each), EARLI (3 samples).


What the variance partition says about repeated measures
From variance_explore (2026-10-13; the numbers are in the DB’s variance_summary):

Time is a small part of the signal factorization sees. In the top 8,000 genes, time plus group × time is 1–4% of variance; between-subject is 35–60%; most of the remainder is within-person variation. Factors fit on a full time-course dataset are therefore mostly person-level structure, the same structure a single timepoint contains (median single-timepoint repeatability 0.25–0.5).
The main biological axis is a stable person trait. Leukocyte composition, which drives PC1 in the RNA-seq data, is 40–70% subject and about 0–7% time.
There is little within-person dynamics to recover. Change between a person’s samples shares no dominant direction (ROSE: its first principal component is 9% of the change) and isn’t explained by composition change; removing each person’s mean would leave factors fit mostly to noise. ROSE’s high residual share comes from noisy low-expressed genes (its subject share rises from 0.08 to 0.34 across expression quartiles).

So the factor analysis fits the full datasets and every per-timepoint subset as they are, and handles repeated measures in how stability is measured and read:

Resampling keeps a person’s samples together (ICA’s bootstrap, above).
Within-family comparisons are not replication. A full dataset and its timepoint subsets, or two subsets, share people: their agreement measures temporal reproducibility within a cohort. Only comparisons between cohorts test replication.
Every factor is described by the same model (factor_vp_<method>_<dataset>, factor_variance_partition()): its sample scores go through the dataset’s variance formula, giving each factor’s share of between-person, time, group, technical and residual variance. A per-timepoint subset uses its parent’s design restricted to its samples, without subject and time terms.

title: Launching the app
text:
Layout
The sidebar holds the choices every page shares: dataset, method and rank (WGCNA: power; the rank defaults to the method’s optimal fit), and the similarity metric (cosine, Pearson, Spearman: which per-factor stability is read). A page has its own selector only when it needs a second dataset or fit (Projection comparison’s target and Fit B, the WGCNA overlap’s other power) or a choice inside the fit (factor, module, field). The Compare settings panel holds what only the Compare page uses: the methods to set side by side and the optimal fit rule.
The Compare page has one tab per question.








Tab
Question
Source




1. Optimal hyperparameter
which rank (WGCNA: power) is best for each method on this dataset
representative fits (v_fits), factors.stability_*, fit_metrics, fit_pairs.ari


2. Best method
which method is best and most stable on this dataset
the optimal fits, plus median projectR R² from projections


3. Across methods
how similar are the optimal factors of different methods
computed live from each optimal fit’s loadings (WGCNA: module membership) and scores


4. Across datasets
how similar are a method’s factors across datasets
projections (sample space) and gene_space_agreement (gene space)

title: Launching the app
text:
Time structure
The first page (before Compare) shows how much of each time-course dataset’s variance is between subjects, an average time effect (the change every subject shares between timepoints), or other within-subject variation (change that differs between subjects, plus measurement noise; the two cannot be separated without technical replicates). It decides how much of what a factor can find is about change over time.

All time-course datasets: the split for each pooled dataset (ANEMONES, CORTICUS, GSE13904, GSE54514, GSE95233, GSE110487, GSE273700), with subjects, samples, subjects measured more than once and timepoints. The whisker is a 95% interval from resampling subjects (the time part is shown without an interval because its interval is unreliable near zero).
Across genes: the distribution of each gene’s between-subject share for the selected dataset’s family, once with every gene counted equally and once weighted by gene variance (which is what the pooled value reflects).
Factors of the selected fit (choose a pooled dataset in the sidebar): the same split of each factor’s sample scores, which separates factors that describe stable differences between people from factors with a within-subject component.

Method. A sample’s timepoint is the sibling dataset whose matrix contains it (config/dataset_families.yml); subjects come from each dataset’s subject_id_col. For each gene (or factor) the sums of squares are split sequentially into subject, then timepoint within subject, then the rest, and converted to variance components with the degrees of freedom each part uses: within = (SS_time + SS_resid)/(N - S); between = (SS_between/(S - 1) - within)/n0, where n0 is the average number of samples per subject; time = max(SS_time - (T - 1) x resid, 0)/N; resid = SS_resid/(N - S - (T - 1)). Raw sums-of-squares shares would overstate the between-subject part (with two samples per subject even pure noise puts about half of the sum of squares there). Pooled values are ratios of sums over genes, so high-variance genes count more. On simulated data with known components the estimates recover them (0.573 against a true 0.58), and with no subject effect the between-subject estimate is 0.004. The split is computed when the page is opened (about 25 s the first time) and cached for the session.
The pipeline now stores the model-based version of this split: per dataset and gene from variancePartition (variance_summary, variance_terms, variance_categories, the variance_partition artifact) and per factor (factor_variance); see Methods, “Repeated measures”. Switching this page to the stored values is pending.

title: Launching the app
text:
Explore fits
A second page (top navigation) shows the sidebar’s method on the selected dataset, across its hyperparameter (One rank in detail uses the sidebar rank). Tabs depend on the method:







Method
Tabs




PCA
variance by rank (reconstruction error, cumulative variance explained)


sPCA
stability vs rank; Index of Sparseness vs penalty with the chosen penalty per rank; one rank in detail


NMF, CoGAPS
stability vs rank; reconstruction error across seeds; one rank in detail


ICA
as NMF, plus ICASSO cluster quality (Iq) by rank


WGCNA
module agreement (ARI) between powers; modules, unassigned genes and scale-free fit by power; for the sidebar power: module sizes and kME of members vs non-members vs the permutation null, the gene dendrogram with module colours, and module overlap with another power



Stability vs rank boxplots each factor’s best match in another same-rank fit, with the chance level (95th percentile of unmatched pairs) marked; ICA separates seed pairs from pairs that involve a bootstrap resample. One rank in detail shows per-factor stability of the representative fit and the seed × seed matrix of mean matched similarity. Cross-rank factor tracking from the old app is not yet ported.

The optimal fit
The DB stores one representative fit per rank but no chosen rank, so the app picks it:

Highest quality that is still stable (default): among ranks whose stability is at least the threshold (default 0.9), the one with the highest in-sample quality. If none qualifies, the most stable rank. Quality rises with rank, so this is the largest rank whose factors still reproduce across seeds.
Highest in-sample quality: ignores stability, so it usually picks the largest rank.

In-sample quality is 1 - mse / val_sd² for PCA, NMF, CoGAPS and ICA; sPCA stores no mse, so its sparse proportion of variance explained is used; WGCNA has no reconstruction, so its mean member kME is used. Quality is comparable within a method, not across methods. Stability is the mean over factors of the median matched similarity across same-rank fit pairs; PCA’s nested components are stable by construction (1), and WGCNA uses the mean ARI against the other powers.
Cross-method agreement matches factors one-to-one (Hungarian, on |Jaccard| of the top 50 genes per factor) and averages the matched overlaps, or clusters samples by each fit’s scores (k = 4) and compares partitions by ARI. Cross-dataset views are ordered by hierarchical clustering with the two directions of each pair averaged.

title: Running the workflow
text:
The main process – tar_make() – coordinates: it submits SLURM worker jobs through crew.cluster and must stay alive until they finish, because workers connect back to it.
As a batch job (anything long, e.g. a full build):
sbatch run_pipeline.sbatch                                     # everything outdated
sbatch run_pipeline.sbatch 'tidyselect::starts_with("fit_")'   # fits only (no ingestion)
sbatch run_pipeline.sbatch 'tidyselect::starts_with("db_")'    # rebuild DB rows from stored results
tail -f logs/targets_main_<jobid>.out
The argument is passed to tar_make(names = ...). targets builds the named targets plus whatever they depend on, and nothing else, so a part of the pipeline can run without the long fits. For example, the repeated-measures analysis alone for every dataset:
sbatch run_pipeline.sbatch 'c(starts_with("design_"), starts_with("expr_"), starts_with("norm_"),
  starts_with("vp_"), starts_with("dream_"), starts_with("de_tables_"), starts_with("dupcor_"),
  starts_with("composition_"), starts_with("controls_"), starts_with("control_factor_"),
  any_of("variance_explore"))'
Check tar_outdated(names = ...) with the same selection first: it lists exactly what would build.
From RStudio Server on the cluster, open the project and use the console:
library(targets)
tar_visnetwork()                            # the graph, outdated targets highlighted
tar_outdated()                              # what tar_make() would rebuild
tar_make()                                  # build everything outdated
tar_make(names = starts_with("fit_pca_"))   # a subset
tar_make(as_job = TRUE)                     # as an RStudio background job
tar_progress_summary()                      # progress while a run is going
An interactive session ends with its SLURM job (16 h at most on interactive), so long runs belong in run_pipeline.sbatch.
Reading results: tar_read(fit_pca_EARLI) returns a target’s value. read_method_fits("EARLI", "spca") (R/targets/run_method_fit.R, available after targets::tar_load_globals()) returns a method’s fits as one list(params, result) per grid row, both sPCA stages included.

title: Running the workflow
text:
SLURM resources
Each method has a crew controller under controllers: in config/pipeline.yml: memory, CPUs, wall time, idle timeout, batch_size, tasks_max. Ingestion, enrichment (fgsea), projections (projectr) and matrix building (prep) have their own. Each controller grows its pool of worker jobs with the backlog and shrinks it when work runs out; a worker is one SLURM job that runs tasks until it’s idle or reaches its time limits.

No worker caps by default. SLURM’s scheduler and per-user limits (200 running jobs per user on HTCF) decide what runs when; a controller without workers: is effectively uncapped. PCA, NMF and ICA keep small caps for efficiency: their tasks take seconds, much less than a worker’s ~30 s R start-up, so one worker per task would mostly be start-up.
Batches. Each branch costs the main process about a second of bookkeeping, so fast methods group grid rows into branches (batch_size), and projections run one branch per (source, target) dataset pair.
Backups for out-of-memory. A controller’s backup: block (crew backup controllers) retries a task whose worker crashed crashes_max times – typically killed for exceeding memory on the largest datasets – on <name>_backup with more memory.
One fit per worker for long fits. sPCA and the vp controller (variancePartition and dream, BiocParallel MulticoreParam over cpus_per_task) use tasks_max: 1, so no long task starts late in a worker’s life.


Main-process memory
The main process’s memory scales with the number of tasks it has handed to crew and not yet collected, not with the data:

Every ready task is pushed at once. targets pushes a ready target to its controller unless the controller is saturated (crew’s saturated(): tasks pushed ≥ workers); a saturated controller’s targets wait in targets’ own backlog as names. Without a workers: cap a controller never saturates, so every ready task is pushed immediately, including the ones waiting in SLURM’s queue behind the 200-running-jobs limit.
Each pushed task carries the globals. The payload is the target plus every object and function that _targets.R and R/ define: about 5.3 MB serialized (2026-10-14), mostly source references. tar_source() parses with keep.source = TRUE; without them it’s 0.44 MB.
It’s held in the main process. mirai’s dispatcher is a thread in the main R process (mirai ≥ 2.7), so each outstanding task costs about twice its payload, ~10.6 MB.

The full run’s opening burst (2026-10-14: about 1,400 tasks, mostly CoGAPS, WGCNA and sPCA, as every dataset’s grids became ready together) took the main process to 14.75 GB within two minutes, and 16.8 GB after twenty. That burst crashed a run with --mem=16G; run_pipeline.sbatch requests more, and up to about 20 GB is acceptable on HTCF. The script also writes logs/targets_main_<jobid>_mem.tsv (the job’s memory, each process’s RSS and the number of worker jobs, every 30 s).
If it becomes a problem, shrink the payload rather than cap workers (a cap below the cluster’s running limit leaves capacity unused when one controller has the remaining work). The targets manual recommends putting a large project’s functions in an R package: each task then ships only the package name, and workers load it. Sourcing R/ without source references would also cut the payload about twelvefold; targets hashes functions without them, so neither change reruns anything.


Tuning
Aim for about 75% average memory and CPU use, never below 50%, and err on the high side. Size memory for the largest dataset (SHIP-TREND: 8,000 genes × 991 samples), not EARLI.

Run the method, e.g. tar_make(names = starts_with("fit_nmf_")).
Find the worker array ids: sacct -X -S <start> --format=JobID,JobName | grep crew-worker.
Check usage with seff <jobid>, or for an array python /scratch/mblab/chasem/seff-array/seff-array.py <array id>. seff-array needs a terminal; from a non-interactive shell wrap it: script -qc "stty cols 100; python .../seff-array.py <id>" /dev/null.

The vp controller also records its own use: norm_, vp_ and dream_ store their job’s cgroup peak memory and CPU seconds in their result ($resources, job_resources() in R/targets/variance.R), and vp_summary_<key> reports them. That was needed when these tasks used socket (SnowParam) workers, which left the job’s process tree so seff missed them; since 2026-10-14 they use forked (MulticoreParam) workers, which use no ports and which seff should count. Compare the two on the next run.
The current values and the measurements behind them are in config/pipeline.yml’s comments.

title: Setup
text:
R and system libraries come from the spack environment /ref/mblab/software/chasem/spack_envs/rstudio-4.6.1. It’s the one rstudio_spack.sbatch launches RStudio Server from, so an RStudio session on the cluster already has it. Outside RStudio, activate it the way run_pipeline.sbatch does:
SPACK_ENV=/ref/mblab/software/chasem/spack_envs/rstudio-4.6.1
eval "$(spack env activate --sh "$SPACK_ENV")"
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$SPACK_ENV/view/lib:$SPACK_ENV/view/lib64${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH}"
unset R_LIBS R_LIBS_USER R_LIBS_SITE
spack here is the one on PATH (spack 1.1); /ref/mblab/software/spack/bin/spack is an old 0.17 install that fails to activate the environment.
spack env activate doesn’t set LD_LIBRARY_PATH, and packages compiled against the environment’s libraries need it. Unsetting R_LIBS* keeps other libraries off the path, so the project’s renv library is the only one in use.
R packages come from the project’s renv library (renv.lock). renv activates automatically from .Rprofile when R starts in the project directory. From a fresh clone:
options(renv.install.timeout = 6 * 3600)
renv::restore()

The renv cache. renv links packages from its cache (~/.cache/R/renv) when a matching build is there, so a restore on a machine that has built them before takes minutes, not hours.
Interrupted installs leave 00LOCK-<package> directories in the project library, and installing that package then fails until they are removed.
The timeout. Everything builds from source against the spack libraries (roughly 300 packages, hours of build time). renv’s default deadline for a whole install is one hour, and when it’s reached renv rolls back the entire batch. Finished builds stay in renv’s cache, so a re-run picks up where it stopped.
.Rprofile turns off two renv start-up checks, synchronized.check (a scan of every project file, about a minute on /scratch) and the sandbox (about 40 s on ~/.cache when 20 workers start at once). Together they took every worker’s R start-up from 68 s to about 10 s. Run renv::status() by hand when you want the check.



CoGAPS is installed from a patched local checkout, not a repository. Its committed configure leaves the autoconf-archive OpenMP macros unexpanded (FertigLab/CoGAPS#150), so built as-is it compiles single-threaded without saying so. The upstream fix (#151) only changes their Dockerfile, so regenerate configure before installing:
git clone https://github.com/FertigLab/CoGAPS.git logs/build/CoGAPS
git -C logs/build/CoGAPS checkout f9075096   # master as installed (3.33.2), after #151
export ACLOCAL_PATH="$(spack location -i autoconf-archive)/share/aclocal"
(cd logs/build/CoGAPS && autoreconf -fi)
Rscript -e 'renv::install(normalizePath("logs/build/CoGAPS"))'
Rscript -e 'library(CoGAPS); stopifnot(compiledWithOpenMPSupport())'
Without spack, install autoconf-archive however the system provides it and point ACLOCAL_PATH at its aclocal directory.
projectR is the feature-add_center_by_loadings branch of cmatKhan/projectR. It adds center_by_loadings, used to project PCA fits. renv records it as a GitHub remote, so renv::restore() installs it.

title: Setup
section: Running elsewhere (without spack, or another scheduler)
text:
Running elsewhere (without spack, or another scheduler)
Nothing in the pipeline depends on spack. Only two places put R on the path: config/pipeline.yml for the workers, and run_pipeline.sbatch for the main process. On another SLURM cluster:

Get R 4.6 however the cluster provides it, e.g. module load R/4.6.1, and run renv::restore() once in the project.
In config/pipeline.yml, give the workers’ setup lines in place of the spack activation:
cluster:
  setup_lines: ["module load R/4.6.1"]
  partition: <your partition, or null>
In run_pipeline.sbatch, replace the spack activation lines with the same module load.
Point data_root (or SEPSIS_DATA_ROOT) at that machine’s copy of the data.

This mirrors the script_lines = "module load R" example in crew.cluster’s documentation. For SGE, PBS or LSF clusters, swap crew_controller_slurm()/crew_options_slurm() in R/targets/controllers.R for crew.cluster’s _sge/_pbs/_lsf equivalents. To run on one machine, use crew::crew_controller_local(). crew.cluster labels itself Experimental/Maturing; targets and crew are mature.

title: Setup
text:
Building these docs
The site is a Quarto website in docs/. Quarto ships with RStudio Server (.../rstudio-server/bin/quarto/bin/quarto); elsewhere, install it from quarto.org.
quarto render docs      # writes docs/_site/
quarto preview docs     # live preview while editing
Rendering first runs docs/build_reference.R, which builds the Function reference from the roxygen comments in the code (it needs the project’s roxygen2).

Documenting functions
Every function carries a standard roxygen block: a title line, a description, @param for each argument and @return. This is a project, not a package, so there are no man/ pages; the blocks feed the reference page instead.
#' Stable identity for a fit
#'
#' Dataset + method + parameters, excluding resource-only settings.
#'
#' @param dataset_id Dataset id.
#' @param method Method name.
#' @param params Flattened parameter list (`flatten_params()`).
#' @param resource_params Parameter names left out of the identity.
#' @return The fit key, `"<method>_<16 hex characters>"`.
fit_key <- function(dataset_id, method, params, resource_params = character(0)) { ... }
Comments never change targets’ hashes, so documenting a function never reruns anything.

title: Overview
text:
This project measures how stable the latent factors found in sepsis gene-expression datasets are, and compares them across datasets. Six methods are fit to every dataset – PCA, NMF, CoGAPS, sparse PCA (sPCA), ICA and WGCNA – across random seeds and across their rank or sparsity parameters. Stability, enrichment, projections and diagnostics are then written to one SQLite database, which a Shiny app browses.
One targets pipeline (_targets.R) does all of it, with the heavy steps running as SLURM jobs through crew.cluster:
targets re-runs only what a change invalidates: editing one dataset’s config rebuilds that dataset only, editing one method rebuilds that method only (Running the workflow).
